entry: Genus of dense, towering vertical [[Cloud|clouds]], abbreviated Cb. Cumulonimbus typically forms from [[Water vapor|water vapor]] condensing in the lower troposphere and builds upward on powerful buoyant air currents. Above its lower portions the water vapor becomes ice crystals, such as snow and graupel, whose interaction can lead to [[Hail|hail]] and [[Lightning|lightning]]. These clouds may be called thunderheads when they cause thunderstorms, and they can form alone, in clusters or along squall lines. Cumulonimbus can produce lightning and other dangerous severe weather, including [[Tornado|tornadoes]], hazardous winds and large hailstones. Normal peaks reach as much as 12,000 m (39,000 ft), and the flat, anvil-shaped top is caused by wind shear or inversion near the tropopause. Cumulonimbus progress from overdeveloped [[Cumulus cloud|cumulus]] congestus clouds and may develop as part of a [[Supercell|supercell]].

Genus of low-level [[Cloud|clouds]] with flat bases and a puffy, cotton-like appearance. The name derives from the [[Latin|Latin]] *cumulus*, meaning "heap" or "pile." Cumulus clouds form by [[Convection|convection]] as surface-warmed air rises and cools until its relative humidity reaches one hundred percent and water vapor condenses on airborne nuclei. They are generally less than 2,000 m (6,600 ft) in altitude unless they develop into the more vertical *cumulus congestus* form. Normally they produce little or no precipitation, but they can grow into *cumulus congestus* or [[Cumulonimbus cloud|cumulonimbus]] clouds. Their development depends on instability, [[Humidity|humidity]] and temperature gradient. A cumulus cloud can consist of water vapor, supercooled droplets or ice crystals, depending on temperature. In one study, liquid water concentration peaked near the middle of the cloud at up to 1.25 grams of water per kilogram of air. Cumulus clouds generally cool the Earth by reflecting incoming solar radiation.

Logo-syllabic [[Writing system|writing system]] of the ancient Near East, named for its wedge-shaped impressions (Latin: *cuneus*). It was in active use from the early [[Bronze Age|Bronze Age]] until the 1st century BC and is the earliest known writing system. It was first developed to write the [[Sumerian language|Sumerian]] language of southern [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamia]]. Writing is first recorded at [[Uruk|Uruk]] at the end of the 4th millennium BC. Over its history the script was adapted to write Akkadian, Hittite, Eblaite, Elamite, Hurrian, Luwian and Urartian. It was rediscovered in the early 17th century through trilingual royal inscriptions at [[Persepolis|Persepolis]] and was successfully deciphered by 1857. An estimated half a million tablets are held in museums, and the largest collection, of about 130,000 tablets, is at the [[British Museum|British Museum]].

[[Oral sex|Oral sex]] act involving stimulation of the [[Vulva|vulva]] with the tongue and lips. The [[Clitoris|clitoris]] is the most sexually sensitive part of the vulva, and its stimulation may result in sexual arousal or orgasm. Cunnilingus may be performed as [[Foreplay|foreplay]] or as an intimate act in its own right. It carries a risk of [[Sexually transmitted infection|sexually transmitted infections]], although the transmission risk, especially of [[HIV|HIV]], is significantly lower than for vaginal or anal sex. Oral sex is often regarded as [[Taboo|taboo]], but most countries do not have laws banning the practice.

Small open container for [[Liquid|liquids]], typically with a flattened hemispherical shape and often a capacity of about 6–16 US fluid ounces (177–473 ml). Cups are made of [[Pottery|pottery]] (including porcelain), [[Glass|glass]], metal, wood, stone, polystyrene, [[Plastic|plastic]] or other materials. Normally they are brought to the mouth for drinking, which distinguishes them from jugs, though a straw or lid may be used. Many have handles, but beakers and small bowl shapes often do not. Cups go back well into [[Prehistory|prehistory]], first as handleless beakers or bowls. High-status cups made of expensive materials have been status symbols since at least the [[Bronze Age|Bronze Age]], and many have been found in burials. Medieval households prized large covered standing cups for toasts, and their form survives in sporting trophies and the chalices of church liturgy. In contemporary English, cups made of glass are mostly called glasses.

Genus of evergreen [[Conifer|conifers]], the cypresses, in the cypress family Cupressaceae. The genus is currently considered polyphyletic, and its New World members have long been uncertain in taxonomy. Cypresses are native to scattered localities in mainly warm [[Temperate climate|temperate climate]] regions of the Northern Hemisphere, including northwest Africa, the Middle East, the Himalayas, southern China and northern Vietnam. Plants grow 5–40 m (16–131 ft) tall, and *Cupressus austrotibetica* can reach 102 m. Many species are adapted to forest fires, holding seeds for years in closed cones until a fire kills the parent tree. In Greek legend, [[Apollo|Apollo]]'s lover Kupárissos was turned into a tree after killing a stag by mistake, and the cypress became a Hellenic emblem of grief. Roman households hung cypress sprigs by their doors in mourning.

Island country within the [[Kingdom of the Netherlands|Kingdom of the Netherlands]] in the southern [[Caribbean Sea|Caribbean Sea]], about 65 km (40 mi) north of [[Venezuela|Venezuela]]. Its capital is Willemstad, and the 2023 census recorded nearly 156,000 residents. Arawak and Caquetío peoples inhabited the island before Spanish explorers arrived in 1499. The Dutch colonized it in 1634, making it a hub of the [[Atlantic slave trade|Atlantic slave trade]]. Slavery was abolished in 1863. The discovery of oil in 1914 made Curaçao a major refinery location, and the island achieved autonomy within the Kingdom in 2010.

Quality related to inquisitive thinking, such as exploration, investigation and [[Learning|learning]], evident in humans and other animals. The term can also refer to an object or event that arouses curiosity; such objects are called curios, and their collections are curiosities. Curiosity drives human development, including progress in [[Science|science]], [[Language|language]] and industry. It is considered an evolutionary adaptation of animals able to learn. Curious animals, including corvids, [[Octopus|octopuses]], [[Dolphin|dolphins]] and [[Elephant|elephants]], pursue information to learn how things function, a behavior called neophilia. Daniel Berlyne identified novelty, complexity, uncertainty and conflict as variables that arouse curiosity, and he also described exploration prompted by [[Boredom|boredom]].

Car-sized [[NASA|NASA]] robotic rover exploring Gale crater and Mount Sharp on [[Mars|Mars]]. It was launched from Cape Canaveral, [[Florida|Florida]], on November 26, 2011, and landed inside Gale crater on August 6, 2012. Its goals include helping determine whether Mars could ever have supported life, studying the role of water, and studying the planet's climate and geology. The two-year mission was extended indefinitely in December 2012, and the rover has operated for more than a decade. Its design served as the basis for NASA's 2021 Perseverance mission.

Capital and largest city of the state of Paraná in southern Brazil (pop., 2024: 1,829,225). It sits on a [[Plateau|plateau]] at 932 m (3,058 ft) above sea level and is the largest city in Brazil's South Region. Its metropolitan area of 29 municipalities has a population of over 3,559,366. The Portuguese founded a settlement on the site in 1693. From the 1850s, waves of European immigrants, mainly Germans, Italians, Poles and Ukrainians, contributed to its economic and cultural development. Its biggest expansion came after the 1960s, with innovative [[Urban planning|urban planning]] that allowed the population to grow from some hundreds of thousands to more than a million. Curitiba is one of 40 Brazilian cities with a very high [[Human Development Index|Human Development Index]] of 0.856, and in 2010 it received the Global Sustainable City Award.

Team [[Sport|sport]] played on ice in which two four-player teams slide heavy, polished [[Granite|granite]] stones toward a circular target called the house. Each team has eight stones, and points go to the stones resting closest to the center of the house at the end of each end. A game usually consists of eight or ten ends. Sweepers using brooms reduce friction in front of a moving stone, allowing it to travel farther and in a straighter line with less curl, so strategy and teamwork are central. The sport is related to bowls, boules and shuffleboard. It originated in [[Scotland|Scotland]], where the first written reference to a contest with stones on ice appears in the records of Paisley Abbey in 1541. The word curling first appeared in print in 1620. Curling has been an Olympic medal sport since the 1998 Nagano Games.

Standardized form of [[Money|money]] used as a medium of exchange. Government-issued fiat currencies include the U.S. dollar, the [[Euro|euro]], the yen, sterling and the [[Renminbi|renminbi]]. Currencies act as stores of value and are traded between nations in foreign exchange markets, where [[Exchange rate|exchange rates]] set their relative values. Originally currency was a receipt for grain stored in temple granaries in [[Sumer|Sumer]] and [[Ancient Egypt|Ancient Egypt]]. By the late [[Bronze Age|Bronze Age]], merchants traded under treaties guaranteeing safe passage, and oxhide-shaped copper ingots may have served as currency. Real coinage appeared after the recovery of Phoenician trade, possibly first in [[Anatolia|Anatolia]] under Croesus of Lydia. Metals were weighed and stamped into coins so that the holder knew the weight of precious metal, which helped lead to banking. Gold coins were used for large purchases, silver for midsized transactions and copper for everyday exchange. Today over 180 national currencies exist, and fiat designs risk debasement through excessive issuance.

Totality of student experiences in an [[Education|educational]] process, often a planned sequence of instruction. Curricula may be tightly standardized or allow a high degree of instructor or learner autonomy, and many countries have national curricula for primary and [[Secondary education|secondary education]], such as the United Kingdom's National Curriculum. Theorists distinguish the explicit curriculum (subjects taught and skills expected), the implicit curriculum (lessons from school culture), the hidden curriculum (what is learned from how school work is organized) and the excluded curriculum (topics left out). Extracurricular activities, including [[Sport|sports]] and [[Performing arts|performing arts]], also form part of it. The word comes from the [[Latin|Latin]] *curriculum*, "a race," and first appeared in English in 1633. [[UNESCO|UNESCO]]'s International Bureau of Education studies curricula worldwide.

Dish with a spicy sauce, originating in [[Indian cuisine|Indian cuisine]] and now internationalized. Medieval Indian proto-curries were flavored with mild spices such as asafoetida, cardamom, coriander, [[Cumin|cumin]] and ginger, with the limited heat of [[Black pepper|black pepper]]. [[Chili pepper|Chili peppers]], tomatoes and potatoes arrived through the [[Columbian exchange|Columbian exchange]] and were a definite step in the development of modern curry. The [[Mughal Empire|Mughal Empire]] introduced subtly spiced dishes, especially in northern India, and Anglo-Indian cuisine developed during the [[British Raj|British Raj]]. Curry spread in the 19th century to the Caribbean and Japan. In India, spices are fried in oil or ghee to make a paste, which may be combined with broth, milk or coconut milk. In Southeast Asia curry often contains a spice paste and coconut milk, while in China and Korea it is based on commercial curry powder. The English word derives from the [[Dravidian languages|Dravidian]] language family, probably from Tamil *kaṟi*.

Expressed wish for misfortune to befall a person, place or object, usually made effective by [[Supernatural|supernatural]] power. When it takes the form of a spell by [[Witchcraft|witchcraft]], a curse is also called a hex or jinx. Many belief systems hold that the curse or its accompanying ritual has causative force, and removing a curse often requires elaborate rituals or prayers. Curses form a significant part of [[Folk religion|folk religion]] and [[Folklore|folklore]]. The "Curse of the Pharaohs" was said to haunt the excavators of the tomb of [[Tutankhamun|Tutankhamun]], a belief popularized by 19th-century British journalists, though [[Ancient Egypt|ancient Egyptians]] did place curse inscriptions on markers protecting tomb goods. In the [[Hebrew Bible|Hebrew Bible]], God and figures such as [[Noah|Noah]] pronounce curses, and long lists warn transgressors of the Law.

Object similar to a [[Line (geometry)|line]] but not necessarily straight. Intuitively, a curve is the trace left by a moving point, a definition given in [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's Elements]] more than 2,000 years ago. In modern [[Topology|topology]], a curve is the image of an interval in a [[Topological space|topological space]] under a continuous function, and differentiable curves require that function to be differentiable. A plane algebraic curve is the zero set of a [[Polynomial|polynomial]] in two variables. Over the [[Real number|real numbers]], an algebraic curve is a finite union of topological curves, while over the complex numbers it is a [[Riemann surface|Riemann surface]]. Algebraic curves over finite fields are widely used in modern [[Cryptography|cryptography]].

City in southeastern [[Peru|Peru]] (pop., 2017: 428,450), near the Sacred Valley of the [[Andes|Andes]]. Founded in the 12th century by Manco Cápac as the capital of the Kingdom of Cusco, it later became the capital of the [[Inca Empire|Inca Empire]]. Spanish forces conquered the region in the 16th century and reestablished the city on March 23, 1534, mostly over Inca monuments. [[UNESCO|UNESCO]] declared it a [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage Site]] in 1983 under the title "City of Cusco." It is a gateway to Incan ruins such as [[Machu Picchu|Machu Picchu]] and hosts over 2 million visitors a year. Cusco is the largest city in the Peruvian Andes, at an elevation of about 3,400 m (11,200 ft).

Unwritten body of community norms treated as binding law. Customary law exists where a legal practice is observed and the relevant actors consider it an opinion of law or necessity (*opinio juris*). Most customary laws concern community standards long established in a locale, but the term also applies in [[International law|international law]] to standards nearly universal in acceptance, such as laws against [[Piracy|piracy]] and [[Slavery|slavery]]. Many customary laws have supporting [[Court|court]] rulings and case law. In indigenous, African and Pacific Island jurisdictions, customary law often governs land tenure, inheritance and family relations, alongside or subordinate to statutory law. In Tswana law, norms are applied contextually and remain open to negotiation. Critics argue that some customary practices conflict with universal [[Rights|human rights]] standards, such as gender equality, prompting efforts at codification.

Tough but flexible, non-mineral outer covering of an organism or part of one, providing protection. Cuticles differ in origin, structure and chemical composition, and the various types are non-homologous. In humans the term is used for the skin around the [[Nail (anatomy)|fingernails]] and toenails and for the layer of dead cells that locks the [[Hair|hair]] into its follicle. In [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]], the cuticle is a multilayered structure outside the epidermis that forms an exoskeleton in [[Arthropod|arthropods]] and [[Nematode|nematodes]]; the arthropod cuticle is mainly [[Chitin|chitin]] with proteins and lipids. In [[Botany|botany]], plant cuticles are waxy, hydrophobic coverings of leaves and young shoots that minimize water loss and reduce [[Pathogen|pathogen]] entry. The sacred lotus resists wetting through its microscopically sculpted surface. In mycology, the cuticle is the outer layer of a mushroom's fruit body.

Eating utensils used for serving and eating [[Food|food]] at the table. Originally the word referred only to knives, while [[Fork|forks]] and [[Spoon|spoons]] were silverware; the three first appeared together as a set in Britain in the Georgian era. The city of [[Sheffield|Sheffield]] in [[Yorkshire|Yorkshire]], England, has been famous for cutlery since the 17th century, and an express train between Sheffield and London was named the Master Cutler after the industry. Sterling silver was the traditional material for good cutlery, [[Steel|steel]] was used for utilitarian knives, and [[Pewter|pewter]] for cheaper spoons. In 1913 British metallurgist Harry Brearley discovered [[Stainless steel|stainless steel]] by chance, bringing affordable cutlery to the masses. Sheffield's counterparts are Thiers in France and Solingen in Germany.

Marine [[Cephalopod|cephalopod]] mollusks of the family Sepiidae, related to squid and octopuses. Cuttlefish have a unique internal shell, the cuttlebone, which controls [[Buoyancy|buoyancy]], and eight arms with two tentacles fitted with suckers. They generally range from 15 to 25 cm (6 to 10 in), and the giant cuttlefish reaches 50 cm (20 in). They are said to be among the most intelligent invertebrates. The Greco-Roman world valued them for the brown [[Pigment|pigment]] released from their siphon when alarmed, and the word sepia now names a reddish-brown color.

Color between blue and green on the [[Visible spectrum|visible spectrum]] of light, evoked by light with a predominant wavelength of 490 to 520 nm. In the subtractive [[CMYK color model|CMYK color model]], cyan is one of the [[Primary color|primary colors]], along with magenta and yellow. In the additive [[RGB color model|RGB color model]], it is made by mixing equal amounts of green and blue light. A dark cyan is commonly known as [[Teal|teal]], and [[Turquoise|turquoise]] is a greenish shade of cyan.

Inorganic [[Chemical compound|compound]] containing the cyano group, a carbon atom triple-bonded to a nitrogen atom (C≡N). The name comes from Greek *kyanos*, "dark blue," reflecting the compound's historical association with Prussian dark blue pigment. The cyanide anion is extremely toxic and causes cyanide poisoning, binding to iron in cytochrome c oxidase and halting aerobic respiration. Soluble salts such as sodium cyanide and potassium cyanide are also highly toxic. Organic compounds with the group, called [[Organic compound|nitriles]], generally do not release cyanide ions, but cyanohydrins do. [[Hydrogen cyanide|Hydrogen cyanide]] is a highly volatile toxic liquid produced on a large scale industrially. Cyanides occur in certain seeds and fruit stones, such as bitter almonds, apricots and peaches, and in [[Cassava|cassava]] roots, where cyanogenic glycosides defend plants against [[Herbivore|herbivores]]. Cyanide is also used in [[Mining|mining]] to extract gold and silver from ore.

Phylum of photosynthetic [[Prokaryote|prokaryotes]], informally called blue-green algae. Cyanobacteria are the first organisms known to have produced oxygen: they split water, release oxygen as a byproduct and use the energy to fix [[Carbon dioxide|carbon dioxide]] into carbohydrates. Over billions of years they changed the early atmosphere, contributing to the [[Great Oxidation Event|Great Oxidation Event]] in the early [[Proterozoic|Proterozoic]] eon. Their photosynthetic pigments include chlorophyll, carotenoids and phycobilins, and their internal membranes, called thylakoids, perform photosynthesis. Plant and algal [[Chloroplast|chloroplasts]] are thought to descend from cyanobacteria acquired through endosymbiosis. Cyanobacteria first appeared in the middle [[Archean|Archean]] eon and are probably the most numerous taxon ever to have existed on Earth. Many species fix [[Nitrogen|nitrogen]] and live in soils or in symbiosis with plants and [[Lichen|lichens]]. Some produce toxins that can harm humans and animals.

Transdisciplinary study of circular causal processes such as feedback and [[Recursion|recursion]], in which the outcomes of actions return as inputs for subsequent actions. The field is named after the steering of a ship, in which the rudder is adjusted in response to its observed effect, forming a feedback loop. The term derives from the [[Ancient Greek|Ancient Greek]] *kybernētēs*, "steersman." Cybernetics arose from exchanges among disciplines in the 1940s and was consolidated at meetings such as the Macy conferences. Early focuses included neural networks, [[Information theory|information theory]] and self-organization. In his 1948 book, Norbert Wiener characterized cybernetics as concerned with "control and communication in the animal and the machine." Its scope later broadened to design, management, sociology and the creative arts. Its ideas about purposeful, adaptive systems are sometimes seen as a precursor to [[Artificial intelligence|artificial intelligence]].
